### What a failed check looks like

A silent `stopifnot` means all its conditions passed. An error names the first
failing condition. The next example deliberately asks for eight rows when the
file has nine; it does not alter `events_raw`.

`tryCatch` catches this expected error and keeps it in `failed_check`, so the
rest of the script can continue. `conditionMessage` reads its message.

```{r}
#| label: failed-check-demo
failed_check <- tryCatch(
  stopifnot(nrow(events_raw) == 8),
  error = function(e) e
)
cat("Error: ", conditionMessage(failed_check), "\n", sep = "")
stopifnot(inherits(failed_check, "error"))
```

The displayed message comes from the actual failed assertion. The final check
passes because the deliberately incorrect assertion produced an error object.
For an unexpected failure, inspect the named condition and its input before
changing anything; deleting the check only hides the problem.

Tables in this chapter display checked output; in R, use `print(object_name)`
to inspect an object. The import output is nine rows and six columns. Each row is **one service event**;
`event_id` identifies that event. A building may have several events. All
response times in this small supplied file are observed; none equals exactly
12 hours. We will therefore need deliberately chosen tests for missingness and
the boundary. These data are synthetic and contain no student information.

## Meeting 2 · Reuse a rule with a contract {#vector-function}

**Slide cues:** “Meeting 2 Question”, “When A Function Helps”, “Function Anatomy”
and “Start With A Contract Sentence”.

A function helps when a meaningful rule repeats, its inputs and output can be
stated clearly, and small tests can check it independently. Do not hide an
unexplained block inside a function just to shorten the main script.

### A vector function

**Commit your prediction first:** write the following sentence as a `# My
contract: ...` comment in your own script, filling all four gaps before opening
either reveal. This is for your own use, not for submission.

> `within_target` accepts …, returns …, treats equality and missingness …,
> and rejects … .

<details>
<summary>Compare the complete contract</summary>

It accepts a numeric response vector and one finite, nonnegative numeric target
(default 12). It returns a same-length logical vector with no missing entries:
an observed response at or below the target is `TRUE`, and a missing response
is `FALSE`. Unsupported response types or invalid targets cause an error.

This matches the teaching contract. It does not promise to reject negative or
infinite response values. Physical-range validation would be an additional
rule, not something `is.numeric` already guarantees. The target itself must
be finite and nonnegative.

**If your answer differed, the likely cause is** mixing up missing responses
with missing targets, omitting the same-length output promise, or forgetting
that equality belongs inside the target.

</details>

Attempt Core Exercise 4 in the starter using your contract comment. Before
expanding, think through the response check and the target checks you
expect to need. Then compare and run the complete reference definition so that
the later test calls can find `within_target`.

**Slide cues:** “Validate Input Type”, “Validate A Default Argument”,
“Calculate Then Check” and “The Last Expression Returns”.

<details>
<summary>Reference implementation · within_target</summary>

```{r}
#| label: within-target
within_target <- function(response_hours, target_hours = 12) {
  if (!is.numeric(response_hours)) {
    stop("response_hours must be numeric")
  }
  if (!is.numeric(target_hours) || length(target_hours) != 1 ||
      !is.finite(target_hours) || target_hours < 0) {
    stop("target_hours must be one finite nonnegative number")
  }
  result <- !is.na(response_hours) & response_hours <= target_hours
  stopifnot(
    is.logical(result),
    length(result) == length(response_hours),
    !anyNA(result)
  )
  result
}
```

</details>

Defining a function stores a rule; calling it applies the rule. The names in
parentheses are arguments. The default `12` is used only when the caller omits
`target_hours`. `result` is local to the call; the final expression returns it.

The abbreviated function-anatomy and default-validation slides are sketches;
use the full checks in the reference version when implementing the contract.

**Optional · Explain this line:** think through why the validation
chain uses `||`, while the response calculation uses `&`.

<details>
<summary>Compare the line explanation</summary>

`||` checks one condition at a time and stops as soon as one is true. Here it
checks type and length before attempting scalar finite/range checks. `&`
combines the two logical conditions entry by entry for the response vector.
This avoids silently recycling a two-element target through the calculation.

</details>

### Choose tests for the mistakes they expose

**Slide cues:** “Known-Answer Test”, “Boundary And Missing Test” and
“Test Expected Failure”.

Think through the expected result before running each call; reuse your earlier
boundary prediction. These are direct function calls; repeating functions over
many inputs belongs to Week 12.

```{r}
#| label: vector-tests
stopifnot(
  identical(within_target(c(4, 18)), c(TRUE, FALSE)),
  identical(within_target(c(11, 12, 13, NA_real_), 12),
            c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE)),
  identical(within_target(c(0, 1), 0), c(TRUE, FALSE)),
  identical(within_target(c(4, 18), 20), c(TRUE, TRUE)),
  identical(within_target(numeric(0)), logical(0))
)
invalid <- tryCatch(
  within_target(c(4, 18), target_hours = -1),
  error = function(e) e
)
stopifnot(inherits(invalid, "error"))
conditionMessage(invalid)
```

`identical` tests exact values and types, suitable for these logical vectors.
For calculated floating-point means, use a stated tolerance or
`isTRUE(all.equal(actual, expected))`. `tryCatch` retains the expected error
as an object, so the test script can continue. An expected error is a successful
test of rejection behavior.

**Read and explain:** which test distinguishes `<` from `<=`? Which detects a
hard-coded default? Which tests the empty output's type?

<details>
<summary>Check your choices and try another invalid input</summary>

The 12-hour equality distinguishes the boundary operators. The call with target
20 checks that the caller can override the default. `numeric(0)` checks that an
empty numeric vector yields `logical(0)`.

**If your answer differed, the likely cause is** testing only a value below the
target: both `<` and `<=` accept that value, so only equality separates them.

```{r}
#| label: invalid-vector-tests
invalid_text <- tryCatch(within_target("4"), error = function(e) e)
invalid_missing <- tryCatch(within_target(4, NA_real_), error = function(e) e)
invalid_infinite <- tryCatch(within_target(4, Inf), error = function(e) e)
invalid_many <- tryCatch(within_target(4, c(12, 20)), error = function(e) e)
invalid_empty <- tryCatch(within_target(4, numeric(0)), error = function(e) e)
stopifnot(
  inherits(invalid_text, "error"),
  inherits(invalid_missing, "error"),
  inherits(invalid_infinite, "error"),
  inherits(invalid_many, "error"),
  inherits(invalid_empty, "error")
)
```

Missing **responses** are allowed; a missing **target** is rejected. Those are
different inputs with different contracts.

</details>

## A table function: one category, one summary row {#table-function}

**Slide cues:** “A Data-Frame Function”, “Check Required Columns” and
“Test Two Arguments”.

### Meeting 2 setup {#meeting-two-setup}

After the import, this block makes Meeting 2 independent of Meeting 1's cleaned
objects. Define `within_target` above before defining the summary function.

```{r}
#| label: meeting-two-data
events <- events_raw |>
  transmute(
    event_id,
    issue = str_to_lower(str_squish(issue_label)),
    response_hours
  )
```

**Begin your implementation first:** for Core Exercise 7, start your own
`summarize_issue <- function(data, issue_name, target_hours = 12)` skeleton with
`# TODO: check required columns`, `# TODO: check issue argument`, and
`# TODO: check selected responses` inside its braces. Think through the inputs,
five output columns and rejected cases before expanding the reference. Complete
your attempt and compare; these stubs are part of the existing exercise, not a
separate written response. Run the complete definition before the tests below.

<details>
<summary>Reference implementation · summarize_issue</summary>

The function receives a data frame with `issue` and `response_hours`, one
nonmissing character issue name, and the target. It returns one row with five
columns. It rejects an absent category or one with no observed responses.
Numeric responses and a valid target are checked by `within_target`.

```{r}
#| label: summarize-function
summarize_issue <- function(data, issue_name, target_hours = 12) {
  required <- c("issue", "response_hours")
  if (!is.data.frame(data) || !all(required %in% names(data))) {
    stop("data must contain issue and response_hours")
  }
  if (!is.character(issue_name) || length(issue_name) != 1 ||
      is.na(issue_name)) {
    stop("issue_name must be one nonmissing character value")
  }
  selected <- data |>
    filter(issue == issue_name)
  if (nrow(selected) == 0 || !any(!is.na(selected$response_hours))) {
    stop("the requested issue needs at least one observed response")
  }
  selected |>
    summarize(
      issue = issue_name,
      n_events = n(),
      observed_responses = sum(!is.na(response_hours)),
      mean_response_hours = mean(response_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
      within_target_rate = mean(within_target(response_hours, target_hours))
    )
}
```

</details>

The explicit missing-issue guard rejects a missing category argument.
The function uses the supplied `data`, rather than silently reading a global
`events` object. It selects rows by the supplied `issue_name`.

**Predict · Think first:** the HVAC and access counts and means from the
raw values. Then run:

```{r}
#| label: summary-tests
hvac_summary <- summarize_issue(events, "hvac")
access_summary <- summarize_issue(events, "access")
stopifnot(
  nrow(hvac_summary) == 1,
  identical(names(hvac_summary),
    c("issue", "n_events", "observed_responses",
      "mean_response_hours", "within_target_rate")),
  hvac_summary$issue == "hvac",
  hvac_summary$n_events == 3,
  hvac_summary$observed_responses == 3,
  abs(hvac_summary$mean_response_hours - 24.5 / 3) < 1e-12,
  hvac_summary$within_target_rate == 1,
  access_summary$issue == "access",
  access_summary$n_events == 2,
  access_summary$observed_responses == 2,
  abs(access_summary$mean_response_hours - 19.5) < 1e-12,
  access_summary$within_target_rate == 0
)
```

```{r}
#| label: formatted-output-2
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(bind_rows(hvac_summary, access_summary), digits = 6)
```

An expected result derived from the input values gives independent evidence.
Copying the function's own output into an “expected” column does not.

### Missingness and failure are part of the result contract

**Predict · Think first:** for two synthetic access events with times `10`
and `NA`, give the number of events, observed-response count, mean and target
rate.

<details>
<summary>Reveal the small test and expected failures</summary>

```{r}
#| label: summary-edge-tests
partial <- data.frame(issue = c("access", "access"),
                      response_hours = c(10, NA_real_))
partial_summary <- summarize_issue(partial, "access")
stopifnot(
  partial_summary$n_events == 2,
  partial_summary$observed_responses == 1,
  partial_summary$mean_response_hours == 10,
  partial_summary$within_target_rate == 0.5
)

all_missing <- partial
all_missing$response_hours <- c(NA_real_, NA_real_)
missing_group <- tryCatch(
  summarize_issue(all_missing, "access"), error = function(e) e)
absent_group <- tryCatch(
  summarize_issue(events, "not-an-issue"), error = function(e) e)
missing_column <- tryCatch(
  summarize_issue(data.frame(issue = "access"), "access"),
  error = function(e) e)
missing_name <- tryCatch(
  summarize_issue(events, NA_character_), error = function(e) e)
stopifnot(
  inherits(missing_group, "error"),
  inherits(absent_group, "error"),
  inherits(missing_column, "error"),
  inherits(missing_name, "error")
)
```

There are two events but one observed response. The observed mean is 10 hours;
the recorded-within-target fraction is `1/2`. The unrecorded time is unknown,
not a measured late response. With no observed response at all, the function
stops rather than presenting an unexplained `NaN` mean.

**If your answer differed, the likely cause is** using the same denominator
for both summaries. The mean response uses one observed time; the flag rate
uses both event rows. A missing response is not evidence that the target was met.

</details>

## Audit a plausible LLM refactor {#ai-audit}

**Slide cues:** “Plausible AI Refactor 1”, “Plausible AI Refactor 2” and
“Refactor Audit”. **Guided practice:** use selectively with Exercise 9.

Use this selective AI-review activity with Guided 9; no live AI account is
needed. Download the
[deliberately flawed review script](downloads/week11-ai-refactor-review.R).
It is a critique target, not a possible solution.

### Shorter code can change the rule

Read this proposed refactor before running it:

```{r}
#| label: flawed-threshold
within_target_ai <- function(response_hours, target_hours = 12) {
  response_hours < target_hours
}
```

Use this test list before opening the evidence:

| Call to the proposed function | Required result under the original contract |
|---|---|
| `within_target_ai(4.5)` | `TRUE` |
| `within_target_ai(12)` | `TRUE` |
| `within_target_ai(13)` | `FALSE` |
| `within_target_ai(NA_real_)` | `FALSE` |
| `within_target_ai(4, -1)` | An error |

**Predict in a comment first:** which tests would fail, and which line explains
each failure? State the generated result as well as the required result.

<details>
<summary>Compare the evidence</summary>

```{r}
#| label: ai-threshold-evidence
ai_evidence <- data.frame(
  input = c("4.5", "12", "13", "NA"),
  intended = within_target(c(4.5, 12, 13, NA_real_)),
  generated = within_target_ai(c(4.5, 12, 13, NA_real_))
)
stopifnot(
  identical(within_target_ai(4.5), TRUE),
  identical(within_target_ai(c(12, NA_real_)), c(FALSE, NA)),
  identical(within_target(c(12, NA_real_)), c(TRUE, FALSE))
)
```

```{r}
#| label: formatted-output-3
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(ai_evidence)
```

The ordinary case passes both functions. Equality and missingness expose two
different changes. The generated version also drops type and target validation.
Repairing `<` alone does not restore the full contract. Restore the validated
`within_target` implementation and rerun the ordinary, equality, missing,
zero-target, changed-target and invalid-input tests.

**If your answer differed, the likely cause is** reading `<` as inclusive, or
assuming R removes missing values automatically. Equality changes `TRUE` to
`FALSE`; the missing response remains `NA`. An invalid target also passes
through without the required error.

</details>

### Does the category argument change the result?

```{r}
#| label: flawed-summary
summarize_issue_ai <- function(data, issue_name) {
  data |>
    filter(issue == "hvac") |>
    summarize(
      n_events = n(),
      mean_response_hours = mean(response_hours)
    )
}
```

Compare these tests of the count and mean before opening the evidence:

| Call to the proposed function | Required count and mean |
|---|---|
| `summarize_issue_ai(events, "hvac")` | 3 events; `24.5 / 3` hours |
| `summarize_issue_ai(events, "access")` | 2 events; `19.5` hours |

**Predict in a comment first:** which call would fail its expected-result test,
and why? Point to the expression that should depend on `issue_name`.

<details>
<summary>Compare two categories and plan the repair</summary>

```{r}
#| label: ai-summary-evidence
generated_hvac <- summarize_issue_ai(events, "hvac")
generated_access <- summarize_issue_ai(events, "access")
stopifnot(
  generated_hvac$n_events == hvac_summary$n_events,
  abs(generated_hvac$mean_response_hours -
      hvac_summary$mean_response_hours) < 1e-12,
  generated_access$n_events == 3,
  generated_access$n_events != access_summary$n_events
)
```

```{r}
#| label: formatted-output-4
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(bind_rows(
  mutate(generated_hvac, requested = "hvac"),
  mutate(generated_access, requested = "access")
), digits = 6)
```

Both return HVAC's three events and mean 8.166667. Replacing the literal
`"hvac"` with `issue_name` repairs argument use, but the abbreviated function
still lacks the full validation and all five output columns. Restore the full
`summarize_issue` implementation above. The two-column comparison here concerns
count and mean only; it is not a claim that the entire output contract matches.

**If your answer differed, the likely cause is** assuming that an argument is
used merely because it appears in the function signature. Trace `issue_name`
inside the body: the filter uses the literal `"hvac"` instead.

</details>

### Optional transfer · A different missing-value mistake

Skip this extra self-check unless it helps you practise Guided Exercise 9.
This abbreviated candidate only computes a category's mean. Test it with two
direct calls, keeping the Week 11 focus on individual function calls.

```{r}
#| label: transfer-variant
mean_response_ai <- function(data, issue_name) {
  data |>
    filter(issue == issue_name) |>
    summarize(mean_response_hours = mean(response_hours))
}
```

**Predict · Think first:** test access times `c(10, 20)` (expected observed
mean 15) and `c(10, NA_real_)` (expected observed mean 10). Which test exposes
the missing option, and why does testing the supplied complete data miss it?

<details>
<summary>Compare the optional transfer test</summary>

```{r}
#| label: transfer-evidence
transfer_complete <- data.frame(issue = c("access", "access"),
                                response_hours = c(10, 20))
transfer_partial <- data.frame(issue = c("access", "access"),
                               response_hours = c(10, NA_real_))
transfer_first <- mean_response_ai(transfer_complete, "access")
transfer_second <- mean_response_ai(transfer_partial, "access")
stopifnot(
  transfer_first$mean_response_hours == 15,
  is.na(transfer_second$mean_response_hours),
  summarize_issue(transfer_partial, "access")$mean_response_hours == 10
)
```

Without `na.rm = TRUE`, `mean(c(10, NA_real_))` returns `NA`. The constructed
partial case exposes the defect; the complete case gives 15 either way.
For this mean calculation, restoring `na.rm = TRUE` recovers 10. The full
summary function's separate all-missing-group guard is still needed.
These assertions verify the candidate's observed defect; it fails the intended
10-hour known-answer test. Keep the full `summarize_issue` as your reference.

**If your answer differed, the likely cause is** assuming `mean` ignores `NA`
by default. It does so only when instructed.

</details>

### Check the repaired workflow against the original

A repair must meet the intended rule, not merely agree with another potentially
wrong implementation. First use independently predicted values; then compare
the original and function-based workflows on the same data. This final
comparison needs the Meeting 1 stages. The reveal below supplies those same
blocks so this page also runs from a fresh session.

<details>
<summary>Rebuild the Meeting 1 checkpoints for this comparison</summary>

If you started Meeting 2 in a fresh session, run these three unchanged blocks
before the comparison. They recreate the same cleaned, derived and summarized
tables; they add no new activity.

```{r}
#| label: clean-events
events_clean <- events_raw |>
  transmute(
    event_id,
    building_id = str_to_upper(str_squish(building_key)),
    reported_at = ymd_hm(reported_at, tz = "Europe/Paris", quiet = TRUE),
    issue = str_to_lower(str_squish(issue_label)),
    severity = factor(
      str_to_lower(str_squish(severity)),
      levels = c("low", "medium", "high"),
      ordered = TRUE
    ),
    response_hours
  )

stopifnot(
  nrow(events_clean) == nrow(events_raw),
  !anyNA(events_clean$event_id),
  n_distinct(events_clean$event_id) == nrow(events_clean),
  setequal(events_raw$event_id, events_clean$event_id),
  !anyNA(events_clean$reported_at),
  !anyNA(events_clean$severity),
  is.ordered(events_clean$severity),
  identical(levels(events_clean$severity), c("low", "medium", "high")),
  is.numeric(events_clean$response_hours)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: derive-target
x <- c(11, 12, 13, NA_real_)
!is.na(x) & x <= 12

events_analysis <- events_clean |>
  mutate(
    within_12_hours = !is.na(response_hours) & response_hours <= 12,
    response_days = response_hours / 24
  )
stopifnot(
  nrow(events_analysis) == nrow(events_clean),
  identical(events_analysis$event_id, events_clean$event_id),
  is.logical(events_analysis$within_12_hours),
  !anyNA(events_analysis$within_12_hours),
  sum(events_analysis$within_12_hours) == 5,
  isTRUE(all.equal(events_analysis$response_days,
                  events_clean$response_hours / 24))
)
```

```{r}
#| label: issue-summary
issue_summary <- events_analysis |>
  group_by(issue) |>
  summarize(
    n_events = n(),
    observed_responses = sum(!is.na(response_hours)),
    mean_response_hours = mean(response_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    within_target_rate = mean(within_12_hours),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(n_events), issue)

stopifnot(
  nrow(issue_summary) == 4,
  sum(issue_summary$n_events) == nrow(events_analysis),
  sum(issue_summary$observed_responses) == 9,
  all(issue_summary$within_target_rate >= 0),
  all(issue_summary$within_target_rate <= 1)
)
```

</details>

```{r}
#| label: preservation-check
reused_flags <- within_target(events_clean$response_hours)
stopifnot(identical(reused_flags, events_analysis$within_12_hours))

reused_summary <- bind_rows(
  summarize_issue(events, "hvac"),
  summarize_issue(events, "access"),
  summarize_issue(events, "lighting"),
  summarize_issue(events, "water leak")
) |>
  arrange(desc(n_events), issue)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(reused_summary, issue_summary)))
```

These four direct calls keep the Week 11 boundary: automated repeated
application is Week 12. Matching this supplied file is useful evidence, but
it cannot catch an exact-boundary or missing-value error when neither occurs
in the file. Keep the small constructed tests as well.

| Contract dimension | Evidence before accepting generated code |
|---|---|
| Inputs and defaults | Check supported types and shapes; override the default |
| Boundary and missingness | Test equality and missing response separately |
| Argument use | Call at least two different categories |
| Output | Check logical type/length or the summary's names and row meaning |
| Failure | Capture errors for an invalid target, absent category and all-missing group |
| Behavior preservation | Compare original and repaired results, plus independent known answers |

When an LLM helps, read every line you accept and explain why it belongs.
Record the suggestion, accepted or rejected changes, and your checks as required
by the existing [AI policy](https://lnajman.github.io/math346/syllabus/ai-policy.html).
Do not upload private student material or assessment keys to public AI tools.
The existing project AI-use appendix remains the project documentation route;
this chapter introduces no separate AI log submission.

**Slide cues:** “Week 12 Boundary” and “Exit Ticket”.

**Individual in-class exit, final five minutes:** for
`within_target(response_hours, target_hours = 12)`, state the input, output,
exact-boundary rule, missing-response rule and invalid-target behavior.
One or two concise sentences; code is optional. Write your own response.

### Self-check (no submission) {#solo-exit-two}

Close earlier reveals. Predict `within_target(c(12, NA), 12)` and explain each
entry from memory. Then predict what changes if the *target* is `NA_real_`.
Think first, then compare below; no written response is needed.

<details>
<summary>Compare the Meeting 2 self-check</summary>

The first call returns `c(TRUE, FALSE)`: 12 is inside the inclusive boundary,
and a missing response maps to `FALSE` under this flag rule. Replacing the
target with `NA_real_` causes an error because the target must be one finite,
nonnegative number. Missing response and missing target have different roles.

</details>

### If you are stuck

| Symptom | Next useful action |
|---|---|
| CSV cannot be found | Run `getwd()` and `file.exists("data/week10-service-events.csv")`; check the project folder and `data/` subfolder |
| `events_clean` or a function is missing | Run the defining block before its first use; restart and rerun in order |
| A starter runs but produces no analysis | TODO lines are comments, so R skips them. Complete the selected blocks before treating the starter as a solution |
| Cleaning creates `NA` | Compare the raw text with the factor levels or timestamp convention; investigate before deleting |
| A check fails | Name the promise it tested, inspect the smallest relevant input, and correct the cause before rerunning |
| A function runs but you cannot explain it | Trace one known scalar, then a vector, equality, missingness and an invalid target; ask for help at the first unclear step |

The optional
[post–Week 10 recovery page](https://lnajman.github.io/math346/weeks/recovery-after-week-10.html)
can help with observation keys and reusable workflows. Stop extending the task
when the selected core work is secure. The routine practice target applies to
the whole week's selected work, not separately to this chapter.
